items.title: Show HN: Slipmark – make AI agents prove what they checked
items.story_key: story|title:slipmark make ai agents prove what they checked
items.content_excerpt: Make AI agents prove what they checked. Bind every agent verdict to a SHA-256 of the files it read, and refuse to ship on mismatch. Set it up in one command: npx slipmark init . Your coding agents then write their sign-off with slipmark attest (see Works with your coding agent ). No model calls, no account, one GitHub Action. A slip mark is the paint line engineers draw across a bolt once it has been tightened and checked. If the bolt ever moves, the line breaks and everyone can see it. Slipmark does the same for AI agent verdicts: once an agent signs off a file, any change after that breaks the mark. Agents now review code, audit specs and sign off their own work. The weak point is the verdict. An agent can report "passed" about a file that has since changed, or that it never looked at, and nothing downstream can tell. We run a nightly pipeline of 20+ agents: research, architecture, security audit, build, QA. Every morning they reported what passed. Then we found the final verification job had been checking the wrong branch for months. It could not fail, so it never did. Months of green ticks, proving nothing. So we built the gate: bind every verdict to the hash of what it read, and re-check before shipping. Pointed at 23 open agent pull requests, it refused all 23. Slipmark doesn't decide whether your agent is right. It makes sure the verdict you are trusting is about the code you are shipping. So pair it with the checks you already trust. Slipmark is the lock on the verdict, not the verdict. If you want stronger verdicts, require more of them: coverage of every changed file, checks Slipmark runs itself, or a re-review when the model changes. Those are on main now ( docs/attestation.md ). Two independent reviewers on sensitive paths, and the rest of attestation v2 , are next. The instructions init writes are enough for agents to attest on their own. We gave Claude Code a plain review task in a fresh repo, with no mention of Slipmark: Both files it based the verdict on, not just the one under review. When the code is fixed, the old verdict stops counting until the agent reads it again. For Claude Code there is also a plugin. items.title: AI agents violate website scraping policies ~97% of the time (NeurIPS2026)
items.story_key: story|title:ai agents violate website scraping policies 97 of the time neurips2026
items.content_excerpt: 1 Pivotal Research, 2 University of Bath, 3 National University Philippines, 4 University of Notre Dame, 5 Hebrew University of Jerusalem ScrapeBench tests whether AI agents follow website scraping policies. The evaluation instructs agents to scrape landing pages and examines how their actions change in response to different legal instructions and policy resources provided in the prompt. The evaluation focuses on websites' terms of service Terms of service (ToS) are a legally binding agreement between a website or app operator and its visitors, governing permitted use of the service. , which can prohibit or restrict scraping activities, and robots.txt A robots.txt file contains instructions for bots indicating which web pages they can and cannot access. Robots.txt files are particularly important for web crawlers from search engines such as Google. files, which stipulate instructions for automated crawlers. Explicitly Prohibited (EP) websites explicitly prohibit scraping in their terms of service or robots.txt. Not Explicitly Prohibited (NEP) websites have no explicit prohibition in either source. The benchmark uses 1,895 high-traffic, English-language websites accessible from the United States, drawn from the February 2026 Chrome Top Million Websites (CrUX) list . The sample contains 1,626 EP websites and 269 NEP websites . In this evaluation, Compliance means not scraping an EP website, while Over-refusal means not scraping an NEP website. Choose a prompt to compare the agents. Switch between compliance and over-refusal to see both measures. We evaluate newer models with ScrapeBench to report progress on compliance with website scraping policies for AI agents not covered in the original paper. Under P1, agents receive only the instruction to scrape the landing page. Compliance ranges from 0% to 11% across the six agents. Under P3, Claude Opus 4.6 exhibits 40.1% compliance and 16.4% over-refusal. Under P5, compliance was 83.6% and over-refusal was 8.2%. On EP websites under P4, GPT-5.2 requested robots.txt in 100% of trials and terms of service in 82.8%. Its compliance rate was 14.2%. We developed a human baseline for our evaluation by studying the responses of 180 human participants who were tasked with making scraping decisions on 15 randomly sampled websites under P1, P4, and P7 conditions. items.title: Skip the DRAM Tier: MoRI UMBP Runs the Agentic KV Cache on NVMe
items.summary: On AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, a MoRI UMBP KV pool on NVMe matched a DRAM pool of the same size within 1% for Kimi-K3 on vLLM, and drives that hold a day of agent KV cost less than DRAM that holds 31 minutes.
items.story_key: story|title:skip the dram tier mori umbp runs the agentic kv cache on nvme
items.content_excerpt: Most of the traffic in agentic serving is multi-turn sessions that resend long prefixes. In the AgentX benchmark replaying real Claude Code sessions, the median turn is 142K input tokens, and over 96% of those tokens are a prefix the server has already seen [3] . A KV cache hit means the prefill node only has to process the small delta. A miss forces a full recomputation of the prefix, which burns GPU time and delays the first token. In our 42 runs of Kimi-K3 on vLLM, raising the KV cache hit rate by 1% of prompt tokens, for example from 95% to 96%, was worth about 10% more throughput (Figure 3). A KV cache hit needs the session’s prefix to still be in memory when its next turn arrives. With dozens of sessions open at once, memory runs out. GPU memory goes first, and host DRAM is the usual next tier. But DRAM fills too: Kimi-K3 wrote 2.3 to 4.6 TB of KV to the pool an hour in our runs, so a 1.8 TB DRAM pool, which lists at about $76,000, holds only the last 23 to 47 minutes of it. That led us to a simple question: why not skip the DRAM tier and put vLLM’s KV pool straight on NVMe? We tried it on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs with UMBP, the KV cache pool in AMD’s open-source MoRI library. At the same size, NVMe matched DRAM’s throughput within 1% on Kimi-K3, in two sets of runs on different machines (Figure 1). On a second workload with longer prompts, NVMe came within 1% of a DRAM pool of the same size. The NVMe pool has no DRAM tier: DRAM only buffers new KV on its way to the drives and stages reads, about 80 GB against the DRAM pool’s 1.8 TB. And NVMe’s cost follows the KV it writes, not the KV it holds, so drives rated for Kimi-K3’s writes cost less than that DRAM pool and hold a full day of KV. “Agentic workloads keep sessions open for minutes or hours, and their KV cache quickly outgrows GPU memory and host DRAM. Results like these, with NVMe keeping up with DRAM at the same pool size, change how we think about sizing KV cache capacity in AI clusters. We’re glad to see this work done in the open, in vLLM and MoRI.” — Dennis Kennetz, Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure DeepSeek already keeps agent KV caches on SSD: the deployment notes for its DeepInfer engine describe three days of retention for agent traffic, on about 14.4 TB of SSD per GPU [4] . This work references DeepInfer for the idea of keeping the KV cache on SSD and for two of its techniques, layer-wise loading and bounded replay, which we test on vLLM below. Figure 1.

items.title: Jcode: High performance coding agent harness written in Rust
items.story_key: story|title:jcode high performance coding agent harness written in rust
items.content_excerpt: High performance coding agent harness written in Rust, built for heavy multi-agent dev workflows High-performance coding agents. Run dozens of agents in parallel without melting your machine. More agents, less RAM, no lag. Want to switch to prereleases (Linux x86_64) and live-update running sessions? Run: Already on a recent build? You can also run jcode update --prerelease (or /update prerelease inside jcode), and switch back anytime with jcode update --stable (or /update stable ). See Update channels and Linux self-dev prereleases . Spawn two or more agents in the same repo, and they will automatically be managed by the server to allow native collaboration. When agent A edits a file that agent B has read (code shifting under its feet), the server notifies agent B. Agent B can ignore it if it is not relevant, or it can check the diff to make sure that it doesn't conflict. Each agent has messaging abilities, capable of DMing just one agent, broadcasting to all other agents hosted by the server, or just agents working in that repo. This allows you to spawn multiple sessions in the same repo, and have all conflicts automatically resolved. Agents are also able to spawn their own swarms autonomously. They have a swarm tool which allows them to spawn in their own teamates to accomplish tasks in parallel. Doing so turns the main agent into a coordinator and the spawned agents into workers. Groups of agents, their messaging channels, their completion statuses, etc are all automatically managed. This can be done headlessly or headed. Supports a wide range of providers , including Claude OAuth and OpenAI Codex OAuth. Jcode is inventing a new form of customizability. One that doesn't limit you to what a plugin or extension can do. Tell your jcode agent to enter self dev mode, and it will start modifying its own source code. Jcode is optimized to iterate on itself. There is significant infrastructure around self development, which allows it to edit, build, and test its own source code, then reload its own binary and continue work in your (potentially many) sessions, fully automatically. items.title: The Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework: Scalable Multimodal UX Attribution in Web Search
items.summary: Sustaining user experience (UX) quality in large-scale web search requires scalable evaluation. Traditional surveys are slow and bottleneck rapid A/B testing, while automated metrics often lack the granularity to diagnose visual-spatial UX anomalies. To address this, we introduce the Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework, a novel industrial architecture for automated UX attribution. Tier 1 (Macro System) acts as a scalable user sentiment regression detector, utilizing a fine-tuned encoder-decoder LLM (based on Gemini XS) on telemetry features. Through multi-task regularization and contextual feature engineering, this tier achieves a +9.8% PR-AUC gain on over 500,000 held-out records, matching baseline recall on all validated regressions with $\sim$20% relative precision gain among the 12 held-out experiments. In production, it reduces measurement latency from weeks to hours and cuts survey overhead by over 40%. Tier 2 (Micro System) provides granular diagnostics by employing a Multimodal LLM (Gemini 3.0 Pro) to natively assess visual renderings and spatial layout of web result blocks, quantifying "User Toil" as the estimated effort required to reach a satisfactory result. Enhanced by RL-based automated prompt optimization and an AI judge for win/loss patterns, the MLLM yields a $>$6.5% F1 score improvement, offering deep insights into content quality and layout friction. Ultimately, this framework enables scalable, accurate, and diagnostic UX attribution, processing O(100k) live experiment queries daily.

items.title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
items.summary: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.

items.title: StereoVLM: Binocular Vision-Language Models for Metric 3D Spatial Reasoning
items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($δ_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.

items.story_key: model:modal|title:how abundant designed efficient rollout architecture with modal sandboxes
items.content_excerpt: Abundant builds reinforcement learning environments that frontier labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta use to train and evaluate their models. Labs improve agent capability by giving them difficult tasks that Abundant designs, letting the model attempt it, and grading the result as pass or fail. Each task is an RL rollout with a full environment. The model needs instructions, a defined goal, and a verifier to decide whether the task was completed. But it also needs infrastructure: compute to power the run, Dockerfiles, and isolation. Depending on the task, an agent may even need accelerators like GPUs. Abundant has created over 75,000 rollouts — ranging from GPU kernel optimization to long-horizon coding — each of which runs in a Modal Sandbox. Modal makes their rollout infrastructure easy to build and cost-efficient to run, enabling the Abundant team to focus on their core business. Today, almost all of Abundant’s rollout platform runs on Modal. Modal Functions power Abundant’s scheduler API to start tasks, clean up dead runs, and review rollouts. Modal Sandboxes power the rollout environments. Abundant initially chose to evaluate Sandbox providers because they wanted to avoid managing EC2 clusters directly, which would pull engineering time away from their core business of building RL environments. Modal enabled them to build their infrastructure directly in code, launch Sandboxes easily via API, and elastically scale their traffic as business grew. As of November 2026, Abundant runs over two million Sandboxes per month. Modal worked with the Abundant team to design and build their rollout architecture, focusing on designing a system that didn’t leave Abundant having to pay heavily for idle compute. Each rollout has a few steps: launch the task, attempt the task, verify the work, and report the work. Throughout the rollout, a “monitor” needs to verify that the Sandbox is still active. While Abundant had considered hosting the monitor outside of the Sandbox, they ultimately chose to include the rollout monitor inside the Sandbox and then used short-lived Modal Functions to start Sandboxes. The small rollout monitor inside the Sandbox makes periodic HTTP calls: a heartbeat every 30 seconds, live events, and the final result. If a Sandbox goes quiet, the control plane will attempt to connect three times before terminating it. items.title: Decision Models for Multilingual Emotion Classification: A Comparative Study Against LLMs and Encoders
items.summary: Decision models receive a question with a closed list of answers and return a probability for each answer instead of free text. They promise low latency and robustness to prompt wording, but no study has compared several of them with fine-tuned encoders across languages. We ask whether systems used without training on labelled data (zero-shot) can replace fine-tuning, and what the decision format adds over a general-purpose large language model (LLM). We compare three decision models (Jev, OpenAI Decisions, Strands Decider 2B) and two LLMs (GPT-6 Luna, Qwen3.5-2B), given Italian instructions, with two fine-tuned multilingual encoders (tabularisai, XLM-EMO) on four emotions (joy, sadness, anger, fear) in 10 social-media datasets in five languages, with paired difference and equivalence tests. The three best zero-shot systems (two decision models and one LLM) score on average about one macro-F1 point below an encoder fine-tuned on the target dataset; our test sets cannot exclude a gap of 4-5 points, and on single datasets either approach wins by up to 22 points. They beat encoders fine-tuned on another dataset by 8-15 points, though against XLM-EMO this may not extend to new datasets, and instructions in each text's language change their results by under 1 point. Exploratorily, they beat the strongest public emotion model used as is by about 6 points. OpenAI's decision endpoint matches GPT-6 Luna, the LLM it runs on, at a fifth of its median latency, and a 2-billion-parameter decision model beats a same-size general LLM by 10 points, owing to its training, not the decision format. The best zero-shot systems, the LLM included, have an SD of about 1 point across prompts. Without labelled data they are a strong default, and decision models add lower latency and, unlike generative LLM use, per-option probabilities. Fine-tuning won by a wide margin only on the largest dataset, GoEmotions.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.328
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added auto mode for Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry and Claude apps gateway; interactive sessions with no permission mode start in it
  • Added "onFailure": "block" for mcp_tool hooks, as for command and HTTP hooks: a hook whose call fails blocks the action
  • Added a warning when a message from a session that skips permission prompts may be held and dropped by a cloud session
  • Added a notice in /status and claude doctor when an OpenTelemetry exporter has no endpoint and its data would likely be lost
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_DEFERRED_TOOL_RESUME, which lets a host stop claude -p --resume and --continue from running a tool call that a hook deferred
  • Added support for apps that embed Claude Code to switch on the policy plugin's allowManagedModsOnly option; an admin's managed settings still win
  • Added a startup warning to the Claude apps gateway when a policy's maxEffortLevel is not a valid effort level
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --repository-folder to name the folder that sessions use for a repository at --capacity 1, in place of its path under the base folder, which can't be a symbolic link
  • Self-hosted runner: Added a start-up warning when the host's settings.json sets a default permission mode that sessions ignore
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --hook-label to claude self-hosted-runner orchestrator, to hand chosen session labels to the spawn-runner hook
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --metadata key=value to claude --environment, to label a session for the spawn-runner hook
  • Self-hosted runner: Added claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_session_queue_wait_by_reason_seconds to the orchestrator's /metrics, so a re-opened session's wait can be told from a new one's
  • Self-hosted runner: Added an orchestrator metric, claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_sessions_given_up_total, that counts by cause how often Anthropic gave up starting a runner for a session
  • Fixed Bash commands in zsh stopping with a "not found" error at a word that starts with =, such as echo ==== or [ a == b ]; =cmd no longer expands to a command's path
  • Fixed automatic compaction reusing the session's earlier system prompt instead of rebuilding it the way /compact does
  • Fixed markdown rendering freezing on some very long or malformed input
  • Fixed rare screen freezes
  • Fixed Esc often being lost at a permission prompt or question when you typed straight after it; in terminals that send Alt as Esc and a key, an unused Alt or Option key now declines there
  • Fixed a paste or a terminal's reply being typed into the prompt when a slow connection cut it in two
  • Fixed saving a scheduled task erasing the project's other saved tasks when the scheduled tasks file can't be read, on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off
  • Fixed a scheduled task with a typo in the project's scheduled tasks file being deleted the next time that file was saved
  • Fixed a case where a resumed cloud session could lose its compaction summary or recent messages when a message was saved late
  • Fixed the token counts on the spinner and for subagents counting a retried reply twice, missing replies that were not streamed, and standing still while Claude thinks
  • Fixed the error shown when usage credits run out mid-response, which named a rate limit
  • Fixed auto mode failing every turn outside Claude Desktop with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS set behind a gateway rejecting betas, on Bedrock, Agent Platform, Foundry or Claude apps gateway
  • Fixed CLAUDE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS not lengthening the 5-minute connection limit on gateways, custom base URLs and cloud providers
  • Fixed some Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers, other than scheduled tasks, ending for good with "Prompt is too long" after large tool results; the largest are now left out
  • Fixed MCP tools whose input schema starts with anyOf, oneOf or allOf going missing on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off
  • Fixed an MCP tool with an invalid input schema failing requests on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off; the tool is now left out and Claude is told why
  • Fixed effort being turned off for a subagent's model for the session if Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Foundry refused its progress summary's effort setting (regression in 2.1.327)
  • Fixed Code Mode stopping a script when a permission prompt outside auto or bypass mode, a plan approval or a question stayed open for ten minutes
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts in auto and bypass-permissions modes failing to call an MCP server that had connected while the previous script was running
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts not running in the background in auto or bypass permissions mode in a session chosen in the claude --resume picker
  • Fixed Code Mode losing a loaded skill, hook context or a note typed with a permission approval when resuming a session in which one reply ran several scripts
  • Fixed Claude not being told that a Code Mode script was cut off when the session was resumed from the picker or in a mode that asks for permission
  • Fixed Code Mode silently using undefined for top-level variables that an earlier failed script never set
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts not being told when a failing command's long output was cut
  • Fixed Code Mode refusing valid scripts that start with a { block
  • Fixed Code Mode refusing scripts that use both a top-level await and a top-level return
  • Fixed an @-mentioned small file not being attached in Code Mode after a script had read or written it
  • Fixed Code Mode offering write() and edit() to read-only subagents that can't call them
  • Fixed Claude starting a turn by itself in Code Mode when Esc was followed by a command such as /model
  • Fixed Claude in Code Mode not being told to run workflows only when you ask, or the workflow size you set in /config
  • Fixed Remote Control repeating the same disconnect message, and telling you to retry a session that can't reconnect
  • Fixed a waiting permission prompt being lost, and its answer ignored, when a remote session restarted while the service was slow
  • Fixed cloud sessions resuming a cleared conversation after a rewind followed by /clear
  • Fixed a remote session losing a turn's tool calls and results when its runner or worker was lost after a dropped model stream had been retried
  • Fixed cloud and Remote Control sessions that just started, or have an @ in their title, being unreachable in cross-session messaging from a session with Remote Control on
  • Fixed Claude being told that cloud sessions can never reply; it now learns when a reply can come and how else to get the result
  • Fixed /diff, the Changes pane of Remote Control sessions and the diff beside an edit leaving out committed work after a command moved into another repository
  • Fixed Remote Control not showing a running workflow's agents when a session run by an IDE extension or other SDK app is opened over an hour after the workflow last made progress
  • Remote Control: Fixed an idle Desktop or VS Code session showing as running after Remote Control is turned on
  • Fixed the model saying background agents were still running after an SDK interrupt had stopped them
  • Fixed Send now in the desktop app and SDK hosts telling Claude that a stopped web search found no results
  • Fixed Cmd+letter being typed into the prompt in terminals that report Cmd
  • Fixed Ctrl+click opening a link twice in GNOME Terminal, side mouse buttons acting as clicks, and the first wheel notch in the other direction being ignored after a pause, in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed Shift+Enter in Konsole outside tmux and ssh, and Alt shortcuts on non-Latin keyboard layouts in terminals that speak the kitty keyboard protocol
  • Linux: Fixed pasting in other apps freezing while Claude Code is suspended with Ctrl+Z, when xclip or wl-copy is installed
  • Linux: Fixed Ctrl+V missing the clipboard image, pasting an old one or hanging
  • Fixed text copied in fullscreen mode including the quote bar, losing spaces at line wraps when a drag scrolled upward, or missing words under the "Jump to bottom" pill
  • Fixed an image path pasted into a ! command becoming an attachment
  • Fixed Ctrl+C showing no exit warning while the ? shortcuts list is open
  • Fixed Ctrl+R search in fullscreen mode and the /theme color editor picking the wrong row when keys arrive together, and keys being dropped there and in the search of /config and /plugin
  • Fixed wrong or missing colors inside GNU screen
  • Fixed many background notifications cutting into the top border of open dialogs in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed a message to a background agent showing a long file path in place of a pasted image
  • Fixed /goal removing a skill's Stop hook, or ending early on another hook's result, when both had the same wording
  • Fixed /bug saying cancelled after the report was sent
  • Fixed Esc not dismissing the transcript share question for Pro and Max users
  • Fixed /hooks losing your place when going back
  • Fixed /export writing a file named .txt when the name was left empty
  • Fixed /terminal-setup in Zed replacing a symlinked keymap.json with a plain file
  • Fixed /install-github-app adding a code review workflow when asked to update the existing workflow file
  • Fixed /plugin reopening a skill, or closing the open page, when a slow save or removal finished after you went back
  • Fixed /plugin asking to uninstall the wrong plugin, or ignoring Esc, after leaving a plugin while a change was still running
  • Fixed typing and arrow keys not working on the /plugin Installed tab after a search with no results or a click on the tab row
  • Fixed holding Enter in /plugin turning off several installed plugins
  • Fixed the /usage plugin total stopping at 2,000 tokens on 1M context models, and low token estimates in /usage and /plugin when no model is picked
  • Fixed Esc on the Bedrock access keys step closing /login instead of going back
  • Fixed /exit and Ctrl+D describing running work differently, and /exit warning about a workflow that had stopped
  • Fixed Claude calling an artifact private after reading one in a shared folder or publishing to another organization's, and saying only named people can open one when its folder's people can too
  • Fixed a plugin's toast sometimes showing another plugin's text
  • Fixed a mod saved just after a turn began sometimes reloading mid-turn instead of at the turn's end
  • Fixed one malformed OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES entry dropping the variable's other labels from metric points, events, and spans. Now only that entry is left off
  • Fixed agent hooks running past their timeout while compacting after a request was refused as too large
  • Fixed a crash at startup when FORCE_COLOR is set to a negative number
  • Fixed a crash in secret masking when the machine is almost out of memory
  • Fixed the Bash sandbox on Linux renaming .git/HEAD after each command when the branch name is not valid UTF-8
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed all running sessions being stopped when a proxy or web filter answered a poll with HTTP 200 and a body such as {}; the runner now retries such a poll
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed deletion of a kept clone's objects or refs, and of commits that existed only there, after a temporary disk error; that start now fails instead
  • Fixed self-hosted runners stopping when their token ran out on a host whose clock is slow or was set back
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed sessions with Anthropic-managed git losing git access to GitHub after a script or hook in the session ran claude again
  • Fixed self-hosted runners with Anthropic-managed git being unable to fetch or push where the machine's git config sets http.proactiveAuth
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a runner that exited without telling the server when setup failed after it had registered; it now deregisters with a reason, and an on-demand runner reports the failed start
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed archiving or requeueing a session not taking effect while it waited for another session to prepare the same repository (--capacity above 1)
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a session with a damaged .claude.json failing every later start under --trust-workspace false; it now starts on defaults, with MCP servers turned off there on again
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a failed start's message losing the words that say what failed when a checkout hook or git printed a lot
  • Fixed the self-hosted runner skipping its post-session hook when a disk stalled for a few seconds; on a dead disk a session's end can take 25 seconds longer by default
  • Fixed self-hosted runners: a session that resumes in a new Claude config directory no longer loses its task list
  • Fixed Claude not being told when a self-hosted session starts without one of its repositories, and why
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed --correlation-id of claude --environment not reaching the spawn-runner hook
  • Fixed the self-hosted runner setup wizard's key rotation advice, which now warns that revoking a key stops the sessions running under it
  • Improved claude -p and SDK sessions to fetch managed-settings plugins that have their own git repository, in the background, for a later session
  • Improved how soon managed-settings plugins from a git marketplace load on a fresh machine in claude -p, SDK and Claude Desktop sessions; a short run may exit up to 30 seconds later
  • Improved the time to resume large sessions
  • Improved memory use when resuming a session with many images
  • Improved memory use and response time in long SDK and desktop sessions that run slow commands or tools
  • Improved Code Mode's speed in auto and bypass-permissions modes by removing a 0.75 second pause after most scripts
  • Improved prompt caching for new Code Mode sessions that have MCP servers, and Claude is now told when a server is still connecting and when the list of servers changes
  • Improved Code Mode's token use with shorter tool descriptions
  • Improved Code Mode to show the command a script is running, and its output, while it runs
  • Improved Code Mode edits: an edit that changes nothing no longer stops a script, and Claude is told where a failed edit matches or comes closest
  • Improved Code Mode: Claude is now told which tool calls were still running when a script failed
  • Improved how Claude starts dev servers in Code Mode's auto and bypass modes: Claude is told to run them as background tasks that show in /tasks
  • Windows: Improved Code Mode by telling Claude that scripts' shell commands run in Git Bash and that PowerShell aliases run instead of functions with the same name
  • Improved starting several in-process teammates at once: far fewer now fail with "Lock file is already being held"
  • Improved the computer use approval dialog: it now shows each app's level of access and plainer warnings
  • Improved cross-session messaging: Claude now explains that Remote Control is off when a cloud session or another computer is not listed
  • Improved claude -p text output to say on stderr when a message from another session is held or dropped, and how to allow it
  • Improved Claude's answers on who can open an artifact it published: Claude is now told to check the artifact again instead of repeating the last publish's answer
  • Improved resumed self-hosted runner sessions: Claude now checks whether its earlier work is still there, and says what is missing
  • Changed plan mode and Bash prompts for Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 on third-party providers to use and offer auto mode, as on newer models; disableAutoMode turns both off
  • Changed Code Mode to no longer run UserPromptSubmit hooks, managed ones included, on scripts' output; to redact that output, use a PostToolUse hook with updatedToolOutput
  • Changed /code-review on most models to report only bugs and CLAUDE.md violations; run /simplify for reuse, simplification and efficiency cleanups
  • Changed /code-review to mark each finding Important, Pre-existing or Nit on most models, and to end each summary with a suggested fix; a clean review's list now reads "Code review found no issues."
  • Changed deniedMcpServers entries of the form claude.ai <name> to apply to that connector in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions too
  • Changed managed PostToolUse hooks to no longer fire for calls refused before they ran: no log entry, rewrite, block or stop there; PostToolBatch gets most, not marked as refused
  • Changed /bug to ask Yes or No before sending, so repeated Enters no longer send a report or open GitHub
  • Changed subagents in claude -p, the Agent SDK, desktop and VS Code to wait for their own subagents by default when CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 is set
  • Changed claude -p with CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 to count a background subagent and those it waits for against one 10-minute wait; raise CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS for longer chains
  • Changed a shell command rewritten by a PermissionRequest hook to a sandbox-excluded command to run outside the sandbox
  • Changed the Claude in Chrome welcome screen and /chrome to say that Claude Code asks before Claude acts on a site, unless your permission mode or a rule in /permissions answers
  • Changed Claude Desktop and Agent SDK sessions on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags off to end the turn when closed with a question open, instead of continuing without an answer
  • Changed pasted text to be marked for Claude as pasted, on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off
  • Changed subagent progress summaries in terminal sessions on the Anthropic API to be written by the default small fast model from short notes, also with telemetry off, using far fewer tokens
  • Changed how a sandbox that can't start is reported, unless sandbox.failIfUnavailable is set: the next sandboxed Bash command is refused and says that the sandbox is off for the session
  • Changed /list-agents to show its list to you alone; Claude lists sessions itself when needed
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed the built-in gh api to be off by default where settings guard Claude's GitHub tools by name; --use-anthropic-gh true turns it on
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed a claude that a wrapper script runs before the session's own claude is up, or after it has ended, to have no Anthropic-managed git
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed CLAUDE_RUNNER_SESSION_UUID and CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE_SESSION_UUID to both be set for the session and its checkout, post-session and spawn-runner hooks
  • Changed self-hosted runners at --capacity 1 to refuse a session earlier when the path of a repository it pushes to is a symbolic link
  • [VSCode] Added a notice when a message from another session is held, with a link to the settings file that can allow it
  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt cutting off its No button, reply field or title when the panel is low or a command, URL or description is long
  • [VSCode] Fixed failed or blocked tool calls showing no reason or a reason cut short, and Glob and Grep counting an error as results

items.title: vllm v0.34.0
items.summary:
v0.34.0

1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new). Thank you!

TL;DR

  • 10 new models (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!)
  • Extensible KV cache is on by default: vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput - in most cases you should now remove gpu_memory_utilization from your configs.
  • Model Runner V1 is gone. Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner.
  • Big speedups on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3).
  • Upgrade check: default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 is required. See Before you upgrade.

Before you upgrade

Important

These changes can break existing setups.

Change What to do PR
Model Runner V1 removed Remove VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0; it now fails at startup. Port V1 logits processors to vllm.v1.worker.gpu.sample.logits_processor. #63373
Default --block-size is 64 (was 16) Pass --block-size 16 to keep the old behavior. ROCm paged attention still uses 16. #63231
Extensible KV cache on by default; gpu_memory_utilization defaults to 1.0 In most cases it's now best to not set gpu_memory_utilization. This should provide maximum kv cache capacity while avoiding runtime OOMs. Use it to share a GPU with other processes or when extensible kv cache is disabled. #56492
ROCm 7.2 artifacts dropped Use the ROCm 10.0 wheels and images. -rocm72 is no longer published. #61939
huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 required Also requires tokenizers >= 0.23.3 and timm >= 1.0.30. #64779
QuTLASS / fp_quant removed fp_quant checkpoints no longer load. #65230
Marlin W4A8 removed Use --quantization humming with VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG instead of VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE. #65542
Keye-VL and Keye-VL-1.5 removed — #64287

All breaking changes, deprecations and new defaults are listed in the full changelog.

New models

Model Notes PR
Mistral Large 4 1T total / 52B active, FP8 and NVFP4. Runs on NVIDIA Blackwell/Hopper and AMD MI350. #64534
MiniMax-M3.1-Flash Blackwell NVFP4 and ROCm kernels, DSpark draft #64111
NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe 30B-A4B speech model: audio chat and /v1/audio/transcriptions #64282
Ricursive Ripple-65B Preview BF16 and NVFP4, ripple reasoning and tool parsers #65745
Zyphra ZAYA1 ZAYA1-8B, ZAYA1-74B-preview #65302
Baidu Unlimited-OCR-2 DASH sparse attention #64016
Liquid AI LFM3, LFM3-VL, LFM3-Audio #65826, #65827, #65828
NVIDIA Canary-1B-v2 ASR and X↔En translation #64215
Ming3-ASR #63585
NVIDIA Parakeet TDT Through the vllm-parakeet-plugin #65005

Highlights

Extensible KV cache, on by default

  • On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free after CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492).
  • Result: a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency.
  • Trade-off: per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache.
  • Hardened with fixes for allocator fragmentation, startup OOMs and KV connectors (#67296, #67485, #66731, #66523, #66197, #65137, #66605, #66674).

Model Runner V2 only

  • Model Runner V1 is removed (#63373).
  • Dual-batch overlap now runs on MRV2, including with speculative decoding and DCP (#61464).

Speculative decoding

  • Suffix decoding runs on MRV2 with a GPU speculator; Arctic Inference is no longer needed (#60339).
  • Custom speculators: declarative configs plus a register_speculative_method plugin API (#63205).
  • CUDA graphs for MRV2 draft-model speculators (#60989).
  • Adaptive verification works with XPress (#65175).
  • Draft KV cache matches the target's dtype, so an FP8 target gets an FP8 draft cache (#65198).

Performance

Improvement Hardware Gain PR
Step5 NVFP4 MoE on TRTLLM-Gen 4×GB200 up to 1.95× decode #65152
GLM-5.3-Flash DeepGEMM FP8 MegaMoE NVIDIA 1.6× output throughput vs DEP4 #60895
Muse Spark Open specialized decode (opt-in) GB300 1.5× single-stream decode #64077
Token-sharded sparse-MLA prefill under TP (default) GB200 GLM-5.3 TTFT 1.24–1.40× faster at 32K–128K #63956
KV-balanced MLA decode for Kimi-K3 (opt-in) GB300 1.34–1.59× decode attention #63638
Qwen3.5 on breakable CUDA graphs (no torch.compile) NVIDIA 3.0–8.8% lower decode ITL #51012
FlyDSL decode monokernel, Muse Spark Open DSpark 8×MI355X +35–57% interactivity at conc. 1–8 #63440

AMD ROCm

  • Release images and wheels are ROCm 10.0 only (#61939).
  • MoRI EPv2 via --all2all-backend mori (#61361).
  • Kimi-K3 specialized decode on MI355X, opt-in (#61435).
  • TRITON_ATTN is the default attention backend on RDNA3 and RDNA4 (#60418).

Serving and operations

  • Checkpoint/restore (CRIU + cuda-checkpoint) through /checkpoint/prepare, /checkpoint/status and /checkpoint/restore, in both the Python and Rust frontends (#62570).
  • Fault-tolerant DP+EP scale-down: dead ranks are removed and their experts redistributed without a restart (#46370).
  • Best-effort NUMA binding on by default (#61258).
  • Opt-in cache-aware admission ordering (#54625).
  • Rust frontend: stateless Responses API (#63902) and n > 1 (#65625).

Install

Python wheels

Platform Install
CUDA 13.0 (PyPI) pip install vllm
CUDA 13.0 (uv) uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=auto
ROCm 10.0 pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/0.34.0/rocm100
XPU uv pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/0.34.0/xpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/xpu --index-strategy unsafe-best-match

Docker images

Platform Image Short alias
CUDA 13.0 (default) vllm/vllm-openai:v0.34.0 vllm/vllm:v0.34.0
CUDA 13.0 + DeepEP over AWS EFA vllm/vllm-openai:v0.34.0-efa vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-efa
ROCm 10.0 vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.34.0 vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-rocm
CPU vllm/vllm-openai-cpu:v0.34.0 vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-cpu
XPU vllm/vllm-openai-xpu:v0.34.0 vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-xpu

latest tags work the same way (e.g. vllm/vllm:latest-rocm). The default CUDA image now includes the AWS EFA userspace (libfabric, aws-ofi-nccl). The -efa image adds DeepEP built for EFA and routes NCCL over EFA by default (#65576).

The Assets section below has the source tarball and the CUDA 13.0 (x86_64, arm64), CPU (x86_64, arm64, macOS) and XPU (x86_64) wheels.

Full changelog

Model support
  • Mistral Large 4 (#64534) runs on MRV2 with:
    • sparse MLA plus the DSA indexer, and cross-layer KV sharing;
    • DSpark, DCP/PCP, NIXL P/D and HiSparse.
  • Other new models:
    • MiniMax-M3.1-Flash (#64111), plus P/D across different prefill and decode TP (#64475).
